utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-69-T. The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution to make its submission in response to the 98 bis submissions of the Simatovic Defence, I just put on the record that we've received a request by e-mail to use slides. Any objection against that? I wouldn't expect any objections. Then apart from that table of confidential exhibits you'd like to deal with briefly in private session, but you also would like to have them marked for identification, is that ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, but I'm not sure we need to go into private session to do that. Ms. Marcus is prepared to address it in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. These are two new documents marked for identification, although I do understand that the content is nothing new, so just that we have a clear record of what you've used. Is the Defence informed about these documents, these tables to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they received the same e-mail that was sent to the Chamber on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps an order to avoid any disturbance of the flow of submissions, would there be any objection against the documents the Prosecution indicated it wanted to have marked for identification? I see a nodding no by the Stanisic Defence. Mr. Bakrac, same for you? Then we can proceed as scheduled. The Prosecution now has an opportunity to make submissions in response to the 98 bis submissions by the Simatovic Defence. Ms. Marcus, you are the first.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours, and everyone in the courtroom. On behalf of the Prosecution, we thank you for this opportunity to respond to the 98 bis motion for acquittal made by the Simatovic Defence. To begin with, I will present to the Chamber some information regarding our submissions today. I will then formally commence our arguments. On the screen before you is a table of contents of our oral submissions. Although each member of the team will address a discrete area of evidence, the Prosecution response is intended as a single response and much of the evidence described by one team member has brought relevance to the entire Prosecution case. I have a few preliminary remarks for Your Honours, prior to the commencement of the substantive submissions. First, the Prosecution's submissions will contain a overview of the evidence in support of the charges in the indictment in response to the Simatovic Defence 98 bis submissions, in particular, their assertion that the Prosecution has not presented evidence in relation to any of the counts in the indictment. Second, the Prosecution does not plan to present a separate segment on the legal standards. Rather, our submissions will be focused upon the factual evidence in support of the charges and how that evidence could support a conviction on all counts by a reasonable Trial Chamber. And thereby why the motion for acquittal should be denied. Third, a motion for acquittal at this stage obliges the Prosecution to marshal its evidence, to facilitate the Chamber's review of the Prosecution evidence and to avoid lengthy recitations of exhibit numbers and transcript references, the Prosecution will rely on a series of demonstrative slides for this purpose. These slides do not contain argument and are not evidence in and of themselves. It is our hope that they will assist the Chamber as well as those transcribing our words. In some cases we have included excerpts of documents and testimony to facilitate the Chamber's review and expedite this process. Also in this regard, although we will not give precise citations for everything we say here, we are able to do so, should the Chamber so request. If there is something that we say which the Chamber would like to have the precise references for, please indicate that and we will be glad to do so. Fourth, for the purpose of clarity the Prosecution will at all times refer to the third amended indictment in this case simply as the indictment. Finally, Your Honours, before I commence, I would like to set out the manner in which the Prosecution plans to deal with confidential evidence, whether that be closed session or private session testimony or under-seal exhibits. The Prosecution has reviewed its submissions fully and is confident that the manner in which the evidence will be presented will fully comply with the protective measures orders of the Chamber. In many instances when it becomes necessary to refer to confidential evidence, the Prosecution rather than asking to go into private session, will simply refer to a table of confidential evidence which was just referred to by Mr. President. This chart lists numbers which will be used by the Prosecution to inform the Chamber which witness or which document was quoted or referred to, without publicly revealing transcript page numbers for closed or private session testimony, pseudonyms of protected witnesses, or the contents of under-seal exhibits. In this respect, Your Honours, I have a brief motion to make. In the filings in relation to Reynaud Theunens, we requested that certain documents be kept under seal because they were pending in the Serbia protective measures litigation. There are -- since that time on the 12th of April, 2010, there has been a motion filed by the government of Serbia in which they explicitly stated that for some of the documents in that we received in response to RFA 219, they do not seek any protective measures. Three of those documents will be referred to in our submissions today. Those three are P1078, P1188, and P1192. The first person to refer to those submissions will be Ms. Friedman, which you can see is section D. We would respectfully request that if the Chamber is able to that we be granted leave to use those, to cite those documents in open session rather than going into private session. But we are in the hands of the Chamber with that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection to the suggestions made by Ms. Marcus? Not. Then, because officially the status has not been changed yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am addressing the parties. Apparently if there's no objection against dealing in public with these exhibits, then may I take it that there's no objection against changing their status into public documents. Apparently all the parties agree. Therefore P1078, P1188, and P1192, the status is changed from confidential into public. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will now commence the Prosecution's submissions. Rule 98 bis, as outlined by Mr. Bakrac, provides that at the close of the Prosecutor's case, the Trial Chamber shall, by oral decision and after hearing the oral submissions of the parties, enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction. The test that has been consistently applied is that a Rule 98 bis motion will succeed if there's no evidence supporting a particular count, or if the only relevant evidence is so incapable of belief that it could not properly sustain a conviction, even when the evidence is taken at its highest for the Prosecution. The Prosecution submits, Your Honours, contrary to the assertions of the Simatovic Defence, that it has presented evidence in support of each count in the indictment. In fact, the Prosecution submits that with respect to all counts in the indictment, the Prosecution has not only met its burden at this stage of the proceedings, but has met its ultimate burden. The Prosecution has presented relevant, probative, and consistent evidence in support of each count in the indictment. Therefore, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that the Defence motion for acquittal must fail. I will now pass the floor to Mr. Travis Farr, who will address Your Honours on the joint criminal enterprise on planning and ordering.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. As Ms. Marcus has indicated, I will focus my remarks on the joint criminal enterprise alleged in the indictment. And I will focus in particular on the evidence of the common criminal purpose of that JCE. This common criminal purpose is set out in paragraph 13 of the indictment as "the forcible and permanent removal of the majority of non-Serbs, principally Croats, Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from large areas of Croatia and B&H, through the commission of the crimes of persecution, murder, deportations and inhumane acts, forcible transfers." The Simatovic Defence denies the existence of this common criminal purpose. At transcript page 11334, they said, "The Defence points out that there is no evidence regarding a joint objective." In addition to challenging the existence of the common criminal purpose, the Simatovic Defence says that there is no evidence that Mr. Simatovic shared any common criminal purpose. That's on the same page. There's been a great deal of evidence in this case that is relevant to JCE, in fact, it is probably not an exaggeration to say that most of the evidence led in this case is relevant to the issue of JCE in one way or another. For the Chamber's reference, slide 3, on the screen before you, contains some of the most important evidence of JCE in this case, some of which will be referred to by my colleagues. Obviously our time today doesn't allow me to discuss all or even most of this evidence. Accordingly, I plan to focus on a relatively small number of pieces of evidence with a direct bearing on the existence of the common criminal plan. In doing so, I will take matters somewhat out of chronological order for ease of presentation. I'll begin with the evidence related to Bosnia-Herzegovina, move on to the SAO Krajina and conclude with the SAO SBWS. Although we've organised our presentation today based on these regions, I want to emphasise at the outset that this case involves a single integrated criminal plan spanning all three regions and several years. We submit that Mr. Simatovic, and the other members of the JCE, always viewed this as a single project and the Chamber should as well. One note about persecutory intent, the common criminal purpose of this JCE involved the permanent forcible removal of non-Serbs. This means that all of the JCE intent evidence that we discuss today is also relevant to persecutory intent. Much of the evidence I discuss will also be relevant to the modes of liability of planning and ordering. Your Honours, before I begin with the evidence from Bosnia, a brief word about the relationship between the accused. The most important relationship between JCE members in this case is the relationship between the two accused. Throughout the indictment period, the accused had a close relationship of co-operation and trust, and this relationship is central to the Prosecution case with respect to both accused. This relationship is demonstrated by documentary evidence, such as the official records admitted as P471, and it's reinforced by the many witnesses such as Milan Babic and Dejan Sliskovic, who stated that Mr. Simatovic was Mr. Stanisic's second in command. Those references are page 12918 and -- of P1878 and paragraph 41 of P441. And Your Honours, I would ask that we move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The most vivid picture of the relationship between the two accused comes from Dejan Sliskovic. Sliskovic had the chance to observe both of the accused's living and working arrangements up close for a period of months during Operation Pauk. He gave evidence that for a period of several months, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic shared an office in the house that served as their command centre and living quarters in Petrovo Gora. That's paragraph 32 of P441. Your Honours, under these circumstances, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic must have shared knowledge and discussed plans and functioned as a single cohesive unit. This is why, despite Mr. Stanisic's having waived his right to make submissions under 98 bis, we will refer to evidence which relates to him. The two men were inseparable and the evidence about their conduct is inextricable. Your Honours, I'll now turn to evidence related to Bosnia. On the 13th and 14th of December, 1993, a critical meeting was taking place in Belgrade, attended by some of the most powerful men in the former Yugoslavia. We know about this meeting thanks to an excerpt from one of Ratko Mladic's notebooks, which has been admitted into evidence as P2532, and this slide, number 4, shows an excerpt from the first page of that exhibit. Your Honours, in our submission, what happened at that meeting is a textbook illustration of joint criminal enterprise as defined by the law of this Tribunal. The first element of JCE is a plurality of persons. The plurality of persons at this meeting in Belgrade included key leaders from Serbia and the Republika Srpska, many of whom were also key members of the JCE charged in this case. The names of JCE members listed in paragraph 12 of the indictment are highlighted in red in the excerpt before you. They include political leaders like Slobodan Milosevic, Radovan Karadzic, and Momcilo Krajisnik. They include military leaders like Ratko Mladic. They include MUP leaders like Mico Stanisic and Radovan Stojicic, aka Badza. Of course Jovica Stanisic was also present, and spoke first at that meeting. Your Honours, as set out at transcript pages 11319, 11321, and 11325 to 326, it is the Simatovic Defence case that Arkan was closely linked to Badza in 1991 and closely linked to Karadzic in 1995. Here we see both of these men at a meeting with Mr. Simatovic's close associate, Jovica Stanisic, in 1993. The second element of JCE is a common criminal plan and the men at this meeting clearly shared a common criminal plan. This is shown by the nature of the discussion, which is basically about two things: First, the extent to which Bosnian Serb forces have established exclusive control over large areas of Bosnia; and second, how that control can be consolidated. A common criminal plan, of course, must be common, and it must be criminal. Jovica Stanisic speaks first at the meeting and his comments are shown on slide number 5. He makes it clear that the goal is a common one when he says to the RS delegation, "We are meeting in order to improve your operational and tactical position and see about help from Serbia." Mr. Stanisic shares the goal of the RS delegation. He wants to know how he can help to achieve it. Karadzic speaks immediately after Mr. Stanisic. He says, "Unification with Serbia is smiling upon us." Karadzic's comments, which are shown in slide 6, also make it clear that the goal of the group is the criminal goal of the permanent forcible removal of non-Serbs from large parts of B&H. He articulates the first strategic objective of the Bosnian Serbs, that is, "to be separated from the Muslims and Croats." His other comments show that this strategic objective refers to physical separation, not to institutional or organisational or cultural separation or whatever other possibilities might be suggested. This is clear from his statement that Serbs are controlling 75 per cent of the territory and controlling the most important parts of the territory. Of course, the Chamber also has before it the evidence of Dr. Ewa Tabeau, Dr. Tabeau's evidence shows the massive population movements that occurred as a result of the pursuit of this goal. Your Honours, we have a plurality of persons and we have a common criminal plan. The next element is contribution. Mladic's record of this meeting shows that Jovica Stanisic contributed to the achievement of this common criminal plan in two key ways. First, he served as a channel of communication between the members of the JCE. Second, he send armed men to help achieve the goal. Mr. Stanisic's prominent role in presiding over this meeting in itself constitutes a contribution to the JCE. This is a singularly clear example of him providing channels of communication between and among the core members of the JCE as alleged in paragraph 15(a) of the indictment. Of course, this exhibit indicates that Mr. Stanisic also contributed to the JCE by sending armed men to help achieve the goal. On page 8 of the English translation of this exhibit, a portion of which we see on slide number 7, Mr. Stanisic says, "We can spare 100 to 120 men." And, "Our combat group is ready to set out tomorrow." Your Honours, General Mladic's contemporaneous notes of this meeting provide a snap-shot of the joint criminal enterprise as it existed on those two days in late 1993. We would submit that as a starting point for analysing the JCE in this case, this meeting proves convincingly that the JCE was alive and well and functioning as charged in the indictment on 13 and 14 December 1993. In other words, Your Honours, the question is not whether the JCE ever existed as all, as the Simatovic Defence has suggested, but rather when it began. One piece of evidence that sheds some light on that question is Mr. Simatovic's speech at the Kula camp awards ceremony in 1997. In that speech, now admitted as part of P61, Mr. Simatovic states that the Special Operations Unit of the State Security Service was formed on 4 May 1991. Mr. Weber will address that exhibit further in his submissions. Another key piece of evidence regarding the evolution of JCE intent is Karadzic's speech before the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo on 15 October 1991, now in evidence as P940. An excerpt of that speech is on slide 8, before you now. In that speech, Karadzic said: "This is the road that you want Bosnia and Herzegovina to take, the same highway of hell and suffering that Croatia and Slovenia went through. Don't think you won't take Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell and the Muslim people in possible extinction. Because, Muslim people will not be able to defend itself, if it comes to war here." Your Honours, a lawfully conducted war, no matter how terrible for the combatants, could never result in the extinction of a people. Therefore, Karadzic's statement before the Assembly of B&H was a threat to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity. Karadzic is saying, in effect, give us the political solution we want or crimes will be the result. He makes this threat precisely by referring to events in Croatia where crimes were already occurring. Why is Karadzic's speech relevant to the intent of Mr. Simatovic in this case? Both of the accused were in touch with Karadzic in the months after he gave his speech. In one of those conversations, Jovica Stanisic expressed almost exactly the same idea that Karadzic expressed in his speech. That conversation took place on the 22nd of January, 1992, and that intercept is now in evidence as P690. We see an excerpt from that intercept on slide 9 on our screens now. In this exchange, Karadzic and Stanisic are talking about what will happen if Serbs and Croats are unable to resolve their disagreements through negotiations. Karadzic says that if the Serbs and Croats are not able to resolve all of their contentious issues, then "They are in for 30 years of torture with blue helmets, with disagreements, with all sorts of things." Mr. Stanisic replies, "With killings." Karadzic says, "I beg your pardon." And Stanisic repeats, "With killings." Mr. Stanisic then says, "We'll then have to push them to go to Belgrade, you know." And a few seconds later continues by saying, "Or we'll exterminate them completely, so let's see where we'll end up." What does this conversation say about the existence of the common criminal plan in January of 1992? The context here is very important. This conversation took place months after the war had started in Croatia, after the fall of Vukovar, and after crimes on a massive scale had already taken place. Large-scale violence was not a theoretical possibility but a present reality. In this context, talk of killings and extermination was not idle pre-war bravado, rather, Mr. Stanisic's statement that "we'll exterminate them completely" was a statement that nothing would prevent the JCE members from reaching their goals. Stanisic's private statement to Karadzic thus echoes Karadzic's public statement in his speech to the Assembly of B&H and expresses the same idea: If we don't get what we want through political means, we will commit crimes to achieve it. Shortly after this conversation, Karadzic also spoke to Mr. Simatovic. P693 is an intercepted conversation between Karadzic and someone identifying himself as Frenki from 6 days after Stanisic and Karadzic had the conversation in which Mr. Stanisic mentioned extermination. During this conversation, parts of which are on slide 10, Frenki tells Karadzic that he is behind him completely. He also says to Karadzic, "You are the main man there, doctor, and that's how it stays." The two of them agree to meet soon. In light of the close relationship between Stanisic and Simatovic, and in light of the relationship between Stanisic and Karadzic shown by the Belgrade meeting and their intercepted conversation, this conversation between Simatovic and Karadzic confirms that all three men were participants in a common project sharing a common goal. Your Honours, I'll now turn to evidence related to Croatia, beginning with the SAO Krajina. Other than the accused, Milan Martic and Ratko Mladic are the key JCE members from the SAO Krajina. Martic in particular played a prominent role in all of the events there and the Prosecution case for the SAO Krajina depends significantly on his relationship with the accused. In that context, there is one key event that clearly illuminates the relationship between Franko Simatovic and Milan Martic and shows the criminal intent of both men. That event is the attack on Lovinac carried out by Mr. Simatovic, Martic, and others in the summer of 1991. Milan Babic discusses this event in his evidence, which is shown on slide 11 and has been admitted as P1877 pursuant to Rule 92 quater. Babic describes how he learned about the attack from Frenki himself. In September of 1991, Babic heard Frenki bragging about the attack in a restaurant in Knin. Describing this, Babic says: "I heard that together with Milan Martic and David Rastovic, and with a mortar platoon from Lapac, he," meaning Simatovic, "had fired at Lovinac, at the police station and at the village itself. I heard from him after these events, I heard him bragging that they had razed it all." Your Honours, in our submission, this clearly shows Mr. Simatovic acting with the goal of forcing the Croat civilian population to leave the SAO Krajina. To put it another way, it is clear evidence that Simatovic intended the permanent forcible removal of Croat civilians. The fact that he and Martic worked together in this attack just confirms that they were working together towards this goal. We would note that this evidence of Babic is corroborated and in fact, in our submission, is greatly strengthened by the evidence set out in the confidential evidence table at B1 through B3. In addition to the Lovinac evidence, there has been significant other evidence led regarding the SAO Krajina with a direct bearing on the intents of the accused and Milan Martic. A great deal of that evidence was led in closed or private session or is under seal, so I would direct the Chamber's attention to confidential evidence table at B4 through B11, with respect to the JCE intent of Milan Martic, and B12 to B13, regarding the JCE intent of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic. The evidence also shows that the accused both maintained extremely close relationships with Milan Martic throughout the times relevant to the indictment. These relationships began before the indictment period and continued throughout it. For example, Milan Babic indicates that he met Jovica Stanisic with Milan Martic near Golubic at the end of August 1990. That's P1878 at page 12930. Babic also indicates that Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Simatovic, and Martic, among others, met at Karadzic's flat in Sarajevo in May 1991. There they were "discussing some maps where the Serbs were in control and areas where they should establish control, or rather, the SDS, Karadzic's party." That's P1878 at page 13082. Other witnesses corroborate and strengthen the evidence of regular meetings between the accused and Milan Martic before and throughout the indictment period. They also describe on-going support for Milan Martic by the accused during this period. I would direct the Chamber's attention to the confidential evidence table at B14 to B19. These witnesses' accounts of the close relationship between the accused and Milan Martic are corroborated by numerous exhibits. One of these exhibits is a greeting telegram sent by Mr. Stanisic on 5 July 1994 for RSK security day, now admitted as P2667. An excerpt of the text is on slide 12 before you. Mr. Stanisic writes: "We are now entering the decisive phase of the fight to achieve the common goals of all the Serbian lands, more determined and prepared than ever before." This, we submit, clearly shows that Mr. Stanisic saw himself as being involved in a joint project with the security forces of the RSK at a time when Milan Martic was president of the RSK. This telegram wasn't the first time that Jovica Stanisic formally acknowledged his relationship with the RSK security forces though. The previous year, that is, in 1993, Mr. Stanisic actually attending the celebration of RSK security day in person. The video admitted as P12 shows that Mr. Stanisic had a front row seat between Milan Babic and Goran Hadzic as Milan Martic addressed those assembled to mark the day. We can see that from the still from that video on slide 13 before us now. The Chamber will recognise Jovica Stanisic, marked with number 2, sitting between Babic, who is number 1, and Hadzic, who is number 3. This still is in evidence as page 3 of P990. The esteem between the RSK security forces and Mr. Stanisic was clearly mutual. P428, which is on slide 14, is a list of individuals who are being awarded security service plaques on RSK security services day. The first name on the list is Jovica Stanisic. Your Honours, in light of this long-standing relationship of support and co-operation between the accused and Milan Martic, it comes as no surprise that Milan Martic would send a new year's greeting letter to Jovica Stanisic. An excerpt of that letter, admitted as page 2 of P995 and on the screen before you now says: "Last year, 1994, was marked by the effort to attain a common stance in our joint effort - the creation of a unified Serbian state." Similar greetings were sent to other members of the JCE, including Karadzic and Krajisnik, two of the men who appear in the photo with the accused that has been admitted as P391 and that is also shown on slide 13. Your Honours, the creation of a unified Serbian state is not if itself a criminal goal, but the methods by which this "joint effort" was pursued by the members of the JCE in this case, including both of the accused and Milan Martic, included forcible transfer, deportation, murder, and persecution on a scale not seen in Europe since World War II. I'll now turn to evidence concerning the SAO SBWS. We've already discussed evidence of the accused's ties to Radovan Karadzic and Milan Martic. Just as Karadzic was a key leader of the Bosnian Serbs and Milan Martic was a key leader of the Serbs in SAO Krajina, Goran Hadzic was a key leader of the Serbs in the SBWS. And I would note that the Simatovic Defence highlighted the links between Hadzic and Arkan at T-11322. Just like Karadzic and Martic, Goran Hadzic had extensive contacts with Jovica Stanisic. Borislav Bogunovic's evidence is that Goran Hadzic went to Belgrade to meet with Jovica Stanisic and Slobodan Milosevic about four times between May and August 1991 and that he would return from these meetings with instructions about how to set up the SAO SBWS government. That's P554, paragraphs 14 to 15 and transcript pages 5973 to 5975. All of the available evidence indicates that Stanisic and Hadzic were discussing the same three things at their meetings that Stanisic, Karadzic, and the others had discussed at the meeting in Belgrade in December 1993: The territory to be brought under Serb control, the goal of ethnic separation, and the means of achieving both. Ms. Friedman will provide additional details on this topic. A key piece of evidence in this regard is Exhibit P403, which you see on slide 16 now before you. P403 is a map of the SAO SBWS prepared with the assistance of a witness who was in a position to have insight into the views of Goran Hadzic, as indicated at B23 and B24 of the confidential evidence table. We submit that the areas labelled "Hadzic's plan" on this exhibit show the parts of the SAO SBWS that Goran Hadzic intended to be brought under control of Serb forces. The portion of P403 labelled "end result" shows the areas that eventually in fact did come under the control of Serb forces. These two areas are the areas outlined in different shades of blue, which are much clearer on the exhibit in e-court than they can be made in this slide. I would observe though that the two areas are substantially the same. Your Honours, this area was brought under the control of Serb forces in the course of a campaign that began with the attack on Dalj in early August 1991 and that was substantially complete with the fall of Vukovar on 18 November 1991. In the course of those attacks, the Croat-controlled towns and villages shown on P403 fell to Serb forces. One quick comment on Vukovar: The indictment in this case no longer charges murders related to the fall of Vukovar. But Vukovar remains relevant to the case in two ways. First, the indictment still contains charges related to persecution, forcible transfer, and deportation from the entire area of the SAO SBWS. Second, Vukovar was a key part of the plan to establish Serb control over the SBWS. For this reason, understanding events related to Vukovar is important to understanding the JCE in this case. This Serb take-over of the SBWS resulted in population movement on a truly massive scale. In that regard, I would refer to the evidence of Anna Maria Radic, particularly page 6 of Exhibit P552 and table 9 of P551. The magnitude of these population movements, while massive, is not surprising in light of the evidence that non-Serbs were forcibly driven out. Some of this evidence can be found in the confidential evidence table at B25 and B26. What was the accused's knowledge of, and role in, this take-over? We submit that the evidence makes it clear that they were aware of this take-over, that they knew precisely what was involved in it, that they supported it, and that they participated in it. A key event in this regard is Jovica Stanisic's visit to Dalj in mid-September 1991. JF-032 described this visit vividly at transcript pages 4659 to 4660. He testified that Stanisic arrived in front of the police station in Dalj in a convoy of four or five vehicles with Belgrade licence plates. He got out of his vehicle and he asked those present where Goran Hadzic was. When he was told that Hadzic was not at the police station, Mr. Stanisic started shouting at those present, asking why Vukovar hadn't fallen yet. He then told the people in front of the police station to find Hadzic and to bring him to Dalj for a meeting. This whole incident took just 40 or 50 seconds, but it speaks volumes about the accused's knowledge of, intentions regarding, and participation in, the events in the SAO SBWS. First, it's significant that Mr. Stanisic came to Dalj. Croats had been forcibly driven out of that very village just a month and a half previously. Second, it's significant that Mr. Stanisic was upset about Vukovar. Vukovar, of course, is a place that Croats would be forcibly driven out of, shortly after Stanisic's visit to Dalj, and the last place in the SAO SBWS to fall to Serb forces. Together, Mr. Stanisic's presence in Dalj and his preoccupation with Vukovar demonstrates that he and Mr. Simatovic shared the goals of Hadzic and others to consolidate control over the region outlined in P403. Perhaps most significant though is Mr. Stanisic's behaviour towards the people in Dalj. When Mr. Stanisic got out of his car in Dalj, he acted like the boss. He expected to be recognised, he expected to be obeyed, and in fact, he was obeyed. Mr. Stanisic's behaviour shows that he was a man with authority in the SBWS. JF-032's account of Mr. Stanisic's visit to Dalj shows that Vukovar was an area of special concern for Mr. Stanisic. How did he deal with this problem? Evidence related to Vukovar, and in particular to Franko Simatovic's role there, is relevant to the Chamber's understanding of the crimes charged. I refer the Chamber to the confidential evidence table at B27 to B29 for that evidence. Your Honours, in light of the other evidence we've discussed today, none of this is surprising. It is not surprising that Mr. Stanisic, the man who in 1993 was offering military assistance to help Karadzic consolidate the Serb take-over and ethnic cleansing of large parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would be involved in exactly the same matters in the SBWS in 1991. Neither is it surprising that Mr. Simatovic, who had personally participated in attack on a Croat village in the Krajina a few months before and bragged about destroying it completely, would now be involved in the attack on Vukovar. Rather, the events in Bosnia and the events in Croatia corroborate each other and show a clear and consistent pattern. This pattern demonstrates that the events in Bosnia and Croatia were part of a single joint criminal enterprise spanning both republics and several years. In light of this pattern, a Trial Chamber could reasonably conclude that Mr. Simatovic shared the common criminal plan to forcibly and permanently remove non-Serbs from large areas of Croatia and B&H through the commission of the crimes charged in the indictment. Your Honours, with the Chamber's leave, Mr. Weber will now address the Chamber on matters related to the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My submissions will focus on the responsibility of the accused for the crimes committed in the SAO Krajina in 1991. During the course of these submissions, the Prosecution will address the significant contributions made by the accused to the JCE through the formation, training, and direction of special units of the Serbian State Security Service and will respond to the Defence assertions regarding the role of these special units during combat operations. The submissions on the special units of the Serbian DB and their relationship to the JNA or VRS are relevant to all counts and specifically to paragraphs 5 and 15 of the indictment. This discussion will involve certain aspects of the JCE in the Krajina and the relationships between JCE members throughout the case. The organisation, training, and support provided by the accused through their direction of special units represented a substantial contribution to the JCE in and of itself. Special units of the State Security Service of Serbia existed between 1991 and 1995. As for the Red Berets, they began as special purpose units of the Republic of Serbia MUP and were later formalised as the JA TD, then the JSO. Initially, they were known in the Krajina as Knindze, and later were commonly known as the Red Berets. This unit served as a key component in the formation and training of other Serb forces, as the term is defined in paragraph 6 of the indictment, and as a highly skilled combat group engaged in operations in Croatia and Bosnia. The origin of special units of the Serbian DB dates to early 1991. According to Exhibit P975, Slobodan Milosevic publicly declared on the 16th of March, 1991: "I ordered a mobilisation of the reserve police forces yesterday. Further engagement and formation of new police forces is to follow, and the government was tasked with preparing appropriate formations to guarantee our security and make us capable of defending the interests of our republic, and also the interests of the Serbian people outside Serbia ..." Shortly after this order, Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic commenced a recruitment and organisation of special units. This task included the engagement of members of the Serbian DB in the formation of new police forces in the SAO Krajina. Evidence of this is reflected in Mr. Simatovic's initial remarks during his Kula speech, which is on the slide before the Chamber. There are two important components of these initial remarks by Mr. Simatovic. First, is the Prosecution's case that special units of the Serbian DB were formed as early as April 1991. Mr. Simatovic, in his speech, unambiguously states that the special units of the State Security Service were constituted on 4 May 1991. Evidence that corroborates the formation of the unit in 1991 is listed on slide 18. Exhibit P1655 includes information which further corroborates the formation date at stated by Mr. Simatovic. Second, Mr. Simatovic's speech shows that the State Security Service of Serbia implemented the task of forming new police forces as described by Slobodan Milosevic. The Prosecution points out one particular aspect of this task. Milosevic stated that the government was tasked with preparing appropriate formations that would be capable of defending "the interests of the Serbian people outside Serbia." Mr. Simatovic parallels this sentiment in the Kula ceremony and stated "where the existence of the Serbian people was directly jeopardised throughout its entire ethnic area." These statements, by two members of the JCE, illustrate in general terms the foundational purpose of the DB special units in 1991. At the inception of special units of the Serbian DB, the accused, and other members of the unit, made a significant contribution to the JCE through the financing, arming, and training of Martic's police, also known as the Krajina Milicija. According to the evidence of Milan Babic, Exhibit P1877 at pages 1539 to 1545, Jovica Stanisic paid for the camp at Golubic that was set up by the Secretary of the Interior of the Krajina, Milan Martic, with the assistance of the State Security Service of Serbia, in particular, Captain Dragan and Franko Simatovic. For further evidence that relates to the material support and financing of Martic's police, the Prosecution refers the Chamber to confidential evidence table at C1 to C10. As part of their support of special units in the Krajina, the accused provided military training to members of Martic's police. At Golubic, recruits came from all municipalities of the Krajina. The trainees were equipped with uniforms and weapons, after receiving training provided by the accused and others with Serbian DB affiliations, the members of Martic's police would go back to their municipalities in order to form special units of the SAO Krajina. This evidence specifically addresses paragraphs 3 and 15 of the indictment. Evidence of the accused's involvement with the training of Martic's police at Golubic is now before you on slide number 19. The Prosecution also refers the Chamber to the confidential evidence table at C9 to C14. The early direct involvement of the accused in the formation and training of Martic's police in the SAO Krajina is evident from evidence pertaining to Dragan Vasiljkovic, also known as Captain Dragan and Daniel Snedden. Captain Dragan worked for the State Security Service in Serbia in 1991 and evidence of his relationship with the State Security Service is now before you on slide number 20. This evidence shows how Franko Simatovic, Captain Dragan and other officials of the MUP Serbia, such as Dragoljub Filipovic, also known as Major Fica, played a leading role in the training of the special police units in the Krajina. For further evidence that relates to the relationship between Captain Dragan and the accused, the Prosecution refers to the Chamber to confidential evidence table at C15 to C17.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: While the starting points of the Red Berets occurred at Golubic, the accused would continue to forge special units of the Serbian DB and mould other Serb forces at training centres throughout Croatia and Bosnia. Mr. Simatovic references many of the training centres during his Kula speech, which is now before you on slide 21. In particular, the Prosecution would note at this time the references to training centres at Golubic; Plitvice; Petrova Gora; Benkovac, which includes the village of Bruska; Lezimir, which is also referred to as Fruska Gora in the trial record; Ilok, which has also been referred to as Pajzos; Doboj; Samac; Bijeljina; and Ozren. After being provided with training and logistical support from the Serbian DB, special units trained at these locations committed crimes. For example, those responsible for crimes in Saborsko were trained at Golubic. This is the evidence of Witness JF-006. JF-047's evidence establishes that the perpetrators of crimes in Bosanski Samac came from Ilok and Lezimir. Similarly, perpetrators of crimes in Doboj received training at Mount Ozren according to the evidence of JF-005. With respect to the special purpose units which would become known as the Red Berets, the Prosecution presented a large volume of testimonial and documentary evidence, including personnel and payment records from the Serbian State Security Service and the evidence of JF-005, JF-031, JF-047, and Dejan Sliskovic. This evidence reflects the composition and activities of the unit between 1991 and 1995, and demonstrates the manner in which special units of the Serbian DB were directed by the accused. For example, Zivojin Ivanovic, also known as Zika Crnogorac. Ivanovic was one of the original members of the unit, and a trainer at Golubic, where he participated in the selection process of the recruits belonging to Martic's police. After this initial assignment, Ivanovic would command units that participated in combat operations in the Krajina, SBWS, and Bosnia. He also was assigned to the camp in Lezimir in March 1992, where members of the unit received training before combat operations in Bosanski Samac. Evidence pertaining to Zivojin Ivanovic can be found on slide 22. Radojica "Raja" Bozovic, who has also been referred to as Kobac. Bozovic was another original member of the unit in 1991. After going to Lezimir, Bozovic would command a Red Beret unit in Doboj in 1992. He would continue his service to the accused as the commander of reserve units of the JA TD during Operation Pauk. Bozovic also participated in operations with Arkan in September 1995. Further evidence pertaining to Raja Bozovic can be found on slide 23. Ms. Harbour will address Mr. Bozovic's role in the crimes committed in Doboj. The Defence argues in part the accused are not responsible for the charged crimes because some of the perpetrators at the time of the offences or at some other point were subordinated to an army, whether it be the JNA or the VRS. Put another way, the Defence is saying the accused are not responsible for the conduct of units they formed, trained, financed through the payment of salaries, armed, supplied uniforms and equipment for, deployed across borders, and directed into combat, because at some particular point they were resubordinated to someone else. This premise ignores the fact that the accused are charged as members of a JCE. It is the Prosecution's case that from 1991 and continuing through 1995, particular units under the control of the Serbian DB operated in co-ordination with the JNA or VRS along with Territorial Defence units and paramilitary forces during attacks on municipalities in Croatia and Bosnia. These attacks were a part of a widespread and systematic campaign to remove the non-Serb population from these municipalities. The co-ordinated use of Serb forces under the control of different JCE members not only shows the existence of a JCE, but also illustrates how members of the JCE implemented their common plan. As a means of accomplishing this co-ordination, the JNA or VRS would form ad hoc joint formations reflecting the combined use of units under the control of the military, the accused and other members of the JCE. The purpose of these temporary formations was to coordinate the activities of different units. As indicated in the testimony of expert Reynaud Theunens at pages 8059 to 8060, these ad hoc formations were established to carry out a specific mission in a specific area during a specific time-period. Accordingly, tactical and operational groups referred to in reports as TGs or OGs, were established because they consisted of several sub-units or elements, which outside the framework of the specific mission do not necessarily operate together. The Theunens report further details materials relating to joint combat operations involving ad hoc formations, including exhibits that discuss Tactical Group 2 in Saborsko in November 1991 at P1575, e-court pages 193 to 196; Tactical Group 17 in Bosanski Samac in mid-April 1992, at P1575, e-court pages 356 to 370; and Tactical Groups 2 and 3 during Operation Pauk at P1575, e-court pages 279 to 280. Your Honours, I don't know if this is a good time for a break, I can further continue if you like.

One thing is however certain, speeding up your speech is not the solution. We'll take a break and resume at quarter to 11.00.
