utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late restart, but there are sometimes other urgent matters to deal with that kept us busy for ten minutes too much. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. From a command perspective, Milan Babic described how this co-ordination operated during the fall of 1991 in the Krajina. This evidence is pound in Exhibits P1877, page 1567 and P1878, pages 13129 to 30. According to Milan Babic, there were two clear chains of command from August 1991 onwards. Slobodan Milosevic was at the head of both. One line went through the JNA. The second line went through Jovica Stanisic and the State Security Service of Serbia who would direct the police of the Krajina, special volunteer units and groups belonging to the State Security Service of Serbia. During joint operations in the Krajina, the units belonging to these two command structures would co-ordinate and subordinate themselves on the ground while engaging in combat operations. As further evidence of Martic's relation to Mr. Stanisic, the Prosecution references witness C-15, who stated on page 1624 that Martic called Jovica Stanisic, "his only and first commander." The Prosecution also refers the Chamber to adjudicated fact 28 from the 28 January 2010 decision in confidential evidence table at C18 to C25 for further evidence of the co-ordination between Martic's police and the JNA. Mr. Farr earlier discussed Exhibit P2532, an excerpt from the Mladic notebooks. There are additional reference to the significant contributions made by the accused in the Mladic notebooks, including Exhibit P2545. An entry from 30 September 1995 documenting a meeting between Mladic, General Perisic, and Mr. Stanisic in Belgrade. During this meeting, Mr. Stanisic references Arkan and discusses how the sending of forces helped in Sanski Most. On 15 November 1995, Ratko Mladic, more directly references Arkan's relationship to the accused during a conversation with Radovan Karadzic in Exhibit P2955. Mladic states that: "Arkan is ... pure MUP of Serbia." Exhibit P2545 together with Mladic's statement about Arkan clearly shows the co-ordination of forces under the control of different JCE members, including Mr. Stanisic. When viewed in conjunction with the evidence presented in relation to the Red Berets, Arkan's Tigers, Martic's police, or the Skorpions, it is apparent that the accused in the Serbian DB retained the ability to direct these units, and the temporary operational subordination of units in co-ordinated combat activities was to advance the JCE's common purpose to forcibly remove the non-Serb populations from areas in Croatia and Bosnia. It is through the co-ordinated use of Serb forces that the accused are responsible for crimes which were planned, ordered and committed in the SAO Krajina. After Slobodan Milosevic's instructions to his government to form new units, the government of the SAO Krajina undertook a series of decisions between April and August 1991, which facilitated the accused and Milan Martic in the recruitment and organisation of special units. These decisions are admitted and many are subject of adjudicated facts. The Prosecution notes a few of these key legislative actions at this time on slide 25. The practical effect of these acts was to further consolidate control of Serb forces in the Krajina under the authority of Milan Martic, which in turn allowed the accused a greater ability to direct these forces that they trained and equipped. At the end of July 1991, Captain Dragan and other members of the unit undertook the leading role in planned combat activities with Martic's police and the Krajina TO. In evidence are a number of reports that document the participation of DB members, the Krajina TO, and personnel from Golubic during the attack on Glina. For example, Exhibit P2658, now before the Chamber, is a report dated 26 July 1991. It is authored by Zivojin Ivanovic. In this report, Ivanovic describes two important aspects of the relationship between the Serbian DB and SAO Krajina units. First, the report states: "Following the instructions and orders that I received from the captain and the core personnel of the Glina Territorial Defence staff command." "The captain" is later identified this in this report is Captain Dragan. This shows that officials from the Serbian DB directed units in the Krajina and co-ordinated their activities with the command staff of the Krajina Territorial Defence. Second, the report states Ivanovic "set off to carry out the task with two squads." In relation to the initial statement indicating the receipt of orders, the second reference indicates that Ivanovic possessed the ability to direct two squads under his command. The Prosecution would also reference the following reports with the accused Simatovic on the addressee list. These are P1121, P1122, and P2671 up to and including P2682. As indicated by expert Theunens at page 1894, such reports were "sent to people who have a need to know the information in order to prepare their decision-making and planning. These people included Franko Simatovic, Milan Babic and Milan Martic, among others." The Prosecution refers the Chamber to confidential evidence table at C23 to C25 for further evidence of Mr. Simatovic's participation in combat activities in the Krajina. The Serbian DB also played a central role in the establishment and organisation of command posts in a system of reporting in the very municipalities where crimes were later committed. For example, Exhibit P1120 is a report dated 23 July 1991 from the Davor municipal war staff. This report indicates that there was a meeting between the defence minister who was Milan Martic as of 29 May 1991, Captain Dragan, and the staff commanders from neighbouring municipalities including Kostajnica. This report includes an assessment by Captain Dragan that "Unity had been established in the conduct of all operations in the area." And concludes: "A system of reporting to the competent organs of the SAO Krajina and the Republic of Serbia have been agreed." This evidence further illustrates the level of co-ordination in the planning of operations between Martic and the Serbian DB. The accused continued to direct and provide logistical support to Martic's police in the Krajina Territorial Defence throughout the fall of 1991. These units, under the direction of the accused and Milan Martic, committed crimes in the Krajina. Franko Simatovic, in his own words at the Kula ceremony, described the relationship between the Serbian DB and the Krajina police in the fall of 1991: "Mr. President, allow us to inform you briefly about the unit's history, its combat record, present situation, and function. When it was formed, its core was made of up of members of our service, Republic of Serbian Krajina police, and volunteers from Serbia. The Second War Service Intelligence Administration, which was also set up at the time, included a special team for offensive and logistical support of the special operations unit. From 12 October 1991, in battles with armed Croatian police forces in the zones of Benkovac, Stari Gospic, Plitvice, Glina, Kostajnica and others, the unit provided important support in the liberation of all areas of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. Around 5.000 soldiers were engaged in these battles and their actions were co-ordinated by the unit command and an intelligence team from the second administration." As members of a JCE, the accused are responsible for committing crimes in the municipalities of Kostajnica, Korenica, Ogulin, Benkovac and Zadar. The horrific nature of these inhumane atrocities is evident from the testimony of the Prosecution's witnesses. The Prosecution notes that many of the facts related to the commission of these crimes in the Krajina are adjudicated. These adjudicated facts are included for the Chamber's reference on the following slides related to the crimes in the specific municipalities. With respect to the Kostajnica municipality, on 20 October 1991, a truck bearing the insignia "Milicija SAO Krajina" brought elderly, unarmed Croat civilians to the Hrvatska Dubica fire station. In total over 40 non-Serb civilians, mostly elderly, were brought to the fire station that day. The following day, 41 of the Croat civilians from the fire station were killed, along with two Serbs. Members of Martic's police are among those responsible for these killings. In the Korenica and Ogulin municipalities near Plitvice, crimes were committed in the villages of Vukovici and Saborsko as part of co-ordinated attacks by the JNA, Krajina TO, and members of Martic's police in October and November 1991. According to the evidence of JF-031, Franko Simatovic and other members of the unit were involved in the participation of combat operations in this area as early as August 1991. Franko Simatovic set up a command centre in the Korenica municipality. This is in the evidence of Milan Babic in Exhibit P1878 at transcript page 13397. Radislav Maksic personally saw both Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic in the Korenica municipality during the fall of 1991. The Prosecution refers the Chamber to confidential evidence table at C26 to C28 for further evidence. On 7 November 1991, local Serb TO units and a special unit from Nis entered the hamlet of Vukovici and killed 9 Croat civilians. With respect to Saborsko, prior to November 1991, at least 20 of the locals from Saborsko went to Golubic and returned to the municipality. They called themselves Martic's police and wore the insignia of the police of the SAO Krajina. In November 1991, Saborsko was attacked by Tactical Group 2, the joint formation of the JNA and SAO Krajina units who included members of Martic's police. In the Zadar municipality on 18 November 1991, the perpetrators of crimes in Skabrnja included individuals who wore uniforms with the words "SAO Krajina" on them. Volunteers from Serbia who were joined to the Benkovac Territorial Defence along with Goran Opacic, who was part of the Benkovac SJB special unit, were present during the attack on 18 November 1991. The Prosecution refers the Chamber to confidential evidence table at C29 and C30 for further evidence. After the crimes in Skabrnja, Goran Opacic receives recognition on the RSK State Security Service day in 1994 along with Jovica Stanisic and Captain Dragan. This Exhibit is P428, which was referenced by Mr. Farr earlier. Further evidence relating to Goran Opacic, his training and relationship to the Serbian DB is included on slide 32. Now before the Chamber is the Prosecution's evidence in relation to the crimes committed in Bruska. Armed men identifying themselves as Martic's men or Martic's Militia came to Bruska almost every day to scare the inhabitants of this village. The armed men called the villagers Ustashas and said that Bruska would be part of a Greater Serbia. One of the hamlets in Bruska was Marinovici was comprised of eight houses. In 1991, the Marinovici hamlet was inhabited by Croats. The killings in Bruska which occurred in the Marinovici hamlet on 21 December 1991 were perpetrated by Martic's police. The Prosecution provides the Chamber with an overview slide with references to the significant contributions made by the accused to the JCE in the Krajina as discussed during these submissions. This evidence directly pertains to paragraphs 3, 5, and 15 of the indictment and relevant to all counts. Through the evidence presented at trial, the Prosecution established that both accused bear responsibility for the horrific events that transpired in the SAO Krajina during the fall of 1991. This evidence alone justifies the denial of the Defence motion pursuant to Rule 98 bis. At this time, Ms. Friedman will present the Prosecution's submissions in response to the SBWS.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has led credible and reliable evidence that demonstrates the accused's role in planning, ordering and committing, through a JCE, the murders of over 60 people and the crimes of persecution, forcible transfer and deportation in the SAO SBWS or Serb Autonomous Region of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Since all counts are encompassed in these charges, the Defence's motion for acquittal should be denied based on the evidence for this region alone. Even before the charged start date of the JCE, Serbia's political leaders, including Mr. Stanisic, were shaping events in what would become the SAO SBWS. Mr. Stanisic's role in planning the events and his participation in a JCE in creating the Serb entity there is evidenced in his meetings with Hadzic and his contribution to the local police force and to arming Serb forces in the region. Mr. Simatovic's role in the JCE is evidenced by his involvement in setting up two camps in the region and the fact that he and his men fought in Vukovar as seen in confidential evidence table B27. Several witnesses have testified that Goran Hadzic met regularly with Slobodan Milosevic and Jovica Stanisic. Before the conflict, Hadzic had been a warehouse clerk. The meetings with Milosevic began as early as May 1990, and continued every step of the way, with the formation of the Serb National Council of SBWS in January 1991, the declaration of sovereignty on 26 February 1991, and the formation of the SAO SBWS government in August 1991. Stanisic was present at approximately four meetings with Milosevic and Hadzic between May 1991 when the conflict broke out in SBWS and August 1991 when the take-over of Dalj, Erdut, and surrounding villages occurred. He was also present at a meeting in Novi Sad in late October or early November 1991, after the Dalj murders had occurred and in the midst of the Erdut murders, to discuss with Hadzic and others the possibility of accommodating Serb refugees in the vacated houses of Croats from Ilok. He clearly knew that the object of the JCE was being achieved. Hadzic would return from his meetings in Serbia with instructions which he would implement. Hadzic conveyed that he had an agreement to establish the government in SBWS and the support of the Serbian government. According to Bogunovic, "The SAO SBWS was a virtual government. It existed in paper but in fact we could not do anything without Serbia's support." And that's at P554, paragraph 19. In addition to advice, Hadzic and his government obtained material assistance from Stanisic and other JCE members in establishing and equipping the police and other Serb forces in the SBWS. Hadzic went to Novi Sad for uniforms, salaries, and advice about setting up police stations. Stanisic himself was at a meeting in late August 1991 where Hadzic got uniforms for the police. Hadzic also received funds for his personal security unit, the SNB, from Serbia, which is seen at Exhibit P504. I will discuss the SNB in further detail later in my submissions. Stanisic also provided support to the SBWS police through a DB operative named Radoslav Kostic. Kostic was employed with the Serbian DB from December 1990. On this point, I refer the Chamber to the confidential evidence table at D1. Kostic issued orders regarding the establishment of the SBWS police, co-ordinated supplies, and was involved in appointing people to the local state security services in SBWS and ensuring that they would report to the Serbian DB in addition to the SBWS chain of command. I refer the Chamber to information in the confidential evidence table at D2, D3, and D4. Jovica Stanisic, through his role as head of the DB, played a significant part in providing arms to the SBWS. Firstly, Stanisic gave Ilija Kojic weapons to distribute in Vukovar around August of 1990. You have heard this from Witness Savic at T-1758 to 1759. Secondly, DB operatives Radoslav Kostic and Lazar Sarac co-ordinated the transfer of arms from Serbia across the Danube, to be stored in Borovo Selo and then distributed prior to the take-over of Dalj as early as April 1991. For further corroboration of Sarac's employment in the DB, I refer the Chamber to the confidential evidence table at D5. The appointment of government ministers in SBWS is a telling indicator of Milosevic and Stanisic's substantial influence over the development of the SAO SBWS. The list of the first ministers appointed is contained in Exhibit P16 which appears on the slide before you. Borislav Bogunovic is listed as the minister of interior, but he has observed that despite this official function, the decisions regarding the police force were taken in Belgrade by others. Bogunovic further testified that when appointing ministers, Hadzic came up with selections which were different from those proposed by the other government members. In some instances, he selected men who were previously unknown to them. Savic said that some of these men arrived in January 1991 from Novi Sad, representing themselves as official representatives of the Serbian government offering their services and assistance, spreading propaganda and discussing proposals for setting up the Serb National Council of SBWS. Hadzic stated that these men were important in order to establish the necessary links to Belgrade and Novi Sad. Returning now to the first person listed on this exhibit, Minister of Defence Ilija Kojic. This is the same man who supplied arms provided by Stanisic and he was appointed to this role on Hadzic's proposal. In November 1991, Kojic was also officially employed by the Serbian MUP while he continued to serve as defence minister in the SBWS government. Kojic's employment in the Serbian MUP is significant. The Defence has argued that the accused are not responsible for actions which are attributed to the Serbian MUP public security as opposed to the Serbian MUP state security. The evidence about Kojic unequivocally rebuts this assertion. An official record suggests that Kojic was employed in the public security and only transferred to the state security in April 1993. The Prosecution refers the Chamber to the confidential evidence table at D6 on this point. However, Ilija Kojic gave a statement to authorised officials of the Republika Srpska MUP. That's P1698. In this statement, he explicitly stated that when he worked in Vukovar, he was an operative of the Republic of Serbia state security. He explained that despite being listed with public security, he was a DB operative, subordinated to the head of the DB, Jovica Stanisic. The statement makes it clear that the distinction between the public security and state security did not prevent them from co-operating and did not prevent Stanisic from tasking at least some of the public security's personnel. Moreover, Stanisic also used Radovan Stojicic, known as Badza, who was the chief of the public security service to achieve his goals. Stanisic and Badza were both appointed to their post on the instructions of President Milosevic to the minister of interior, Zoran Sokolovic. I refer Your Honours to the confidential evidence table at D7. Further, General Milovanovic testified at T-4383 to 4386 that Badza himself referred to Stanisic as his boss, and Bogunovic testified at T-6061 that Hadzic saw Stanisic as the link between Milosevic and Badza. Stanisic relied on Badza to command the TO and on Arkan to fight with the JNA in joint operations and to wreak havoc on the civilian population. I will discuss the role, the specific role of each man in turn. Badza, deputy minister of the interior, a JCE member and someone who considered Stanisic to be his boss, was already present in the SBWS when the take-over operations in Dalj and Erdut began. He attended government meetings, demanded to be informed of everything, and even gave orders to the minister of interior. Badza was sent in order to ensure that actions were undertaken in accordance with the common plan, and in fact, his title suggests that he had the authority to do just that. His official title was the commander of the TO of the SAO SBWS, as seen in a certificate admitted at P54, but more significantly, he announced himself as, "the commander to one and all" to the local police forces and TO, according to the evidence noted at confidential evidence table D8. He made it clear that there would be no independent leadership among the local TO and police, that it would all be co-ordinated and monitored from the headquarters in Erdut. Badza's intent to be the central co-ordinator is also clear in subsequent events. When Bogunovic, the minister of interior would not report daily to him and would not agree to closer contact with Badza than with the JNA, Badza influenced Hadzic to remove Bogunovic from office. And that's at P553, paragraph 73. Badza influenced the events in the region in several key ways. First, the meeting he held in Erdut, when he announced himself as the commander, focused on sending SBWS forces to Vukovar, which was envisioned at capital of the RSK, Republika Srpska Krajina, which would be formed. Second, he tasked his deputy, a man named Miodrag Zavisic, with establishing police offices in villages. Third, with him were about 60 to 70 men who were Special Police force from Serbia. C-15 testified that because Badza's men were trained for special operations, they would be the ones to lead TO units into operations. Fourthly, he assisted in acquiring uniforms and equipment for the SBWS police in Novi Sad. And finally, he played a role in planning and facilitating Arkan's crimes, as I will discuss in greater detail. Stanisic sent Arkan, a JCE member, to the SBWS before the take-overs and Arkan established his training centre and base in Erdut. He had 50 or 60 men at first, but eventually had about 2 to 300 men under his command. The Defence have argued that Arkan was subordinated to the JNA and SBWS and that he was not connected to Stanisic and Simatovic. Your Honours, the Prosecution's case is that Arkan, like other units of the Serbian DB, did at times participate in operations under joint command of the JNA, and that these co-ordinated operations were in keeping with the intent of the JCE. The evidence also demonstrates that Arkan acted separately from the JNA in committing the murders charged in Dalj and Erdut, and that these actions were also the intent of the JCE. In May 1991, Arkan himself openly stated that Jovica Stanisic was his boss. This was confirmed by Radmilo Bogdanovic, the minister of interior of Serbia and another JCE member, who stated that they sent Arkan to the region as a commander. This evidence was provided by Witness Savic. Stanisic not only sent Arkan to the region, he also supplied Arkan's training centre with weapons and ammunition as indicated in Exhibit D31. And ensured that Arkan could move around freely, as announced by Badza at the meeting mentioned earlier, and described in greater detail in the confidential evidence table at D9. Further, Arkan's training centre, where he beat and killed many civilians, was funded by the SBWS government, as Your Honours can find in Exhibit P332 and P1187. The evidence also demonstrates that the SBWS government was itself heavily influenced and funded by Serbia, for example, at P968. Arkan engaged in a a widespread and systematic attack of violence and terror on the civilian populations of Dalj and Erdut. JF-032 described at T-4688 how Arkan's Men would do as they please and bring people to the training centre at will. He referred to them as "the executioners." Slide 40 identifies key evidence Your Honours have heard and admitted in relation to the crimes in Dalj. The first of the two mass executions charged in Dalj occurred on the night of the 21st of September, 1991. On this night, Arkan and Hadzic arrived in the police building. They removed the two men who had connections to prominent Serbs, and then Arkan's Men murdered the remaining non-Serb detainees. The details of the crime were documented in a contemporaneous police report about the removal of the men from the prison and has been admitted as P10. The second mass execution charged in Dalj occurred on the night of the 4th of October when Arkan and his men, including Milorad Stricevic, shot the non-Serb civilians held in the Dalj police building and dumped the bodies in the Danube. Documentary evidence of this incident includes both the contemporaneous police report, P11, drafted by local policemen who eventually resigned, as well as a certificate signed by Milorad Stricevic, stating that he had removed the prisoners, P315. One of the listed recipients of the seconds report was Badza's deputy. Following this incident, the local population demanded accountability. Arkan held a speech and took responsibility for the crimes. He said that no one could do anything to him and that he operated with the policy "a tooth for a tooth and an eye for an eye." The rest of the SAO SBWS murders were perpetrated in Erdut, mostly at Arkan's training centre, and the bodies were dumped in mass graves or wells. Slide 41 identifies the key evidence in relation to these crimes. Between November 1991 and June 1992, Arkan's Men, along with the SBWS TO and local police rounded up Croats and ethnic Hungarians in Erdut, Dalj, and Klisa, bringing them to Arkan's training centre in Erdut, where they were interrogated, beaten, threatened and in many cases they were ultimately murdered. The record is replete with firsthand evidence of civilians who suffered this brutality themselves and whose own families and neighbours were arrested and killed. The evidence has shown that the non-Serb population of Dalj, Erdut and the SBWS region was deported and forcibly transferred by the members of the JCE and the armed forces that they used as their tools. Many civilians were literally put on buses and expelled, while others fled due to the coercive and threatening circumstances. The first arrests and forcible transfer of non-Serbs began in July 1991 with subsequent waves occurring after the take-over of Dalj and Erdut in August 1991, the fall of Vukovar in November 1991, and in April 1992 when Arkan's Men deported a number of elderly villagers who had remained in Erdut. Many of the villagers who initially stayed in their homes after the take-over, such as Luka Sutalo and C-1118 were subjected to such terrible conditions that eventually they too fled. Sutalo described how he feared for his life and applied for a permit to leave, which was granted only after he had signed over his property to the village council. At T-3991, Sutalo described the searches and interrogations and concluded by stating, "We had no rights, we weren't given any food, any clothes and we realised we couldn't survive there, that we had to flee." Some of the villagers who fled when Dalj and Erdut were originally taken over returned, especially the small community of ethnic Hungarians from Dalj who believed that they could stay in their homes. However, once their family members disappeared, the fear and sorrow was too great and they too fled. This is a pattern that Your Honours will hear Ms. Harbour and Ms. Marcus refer to in relation to events in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The facts clearly demonstrate the persecutory intent in the murders and forced displacements that took place in SBWS. The vast majority of those killed were non-Serbs and you've heard evidence from JF-015, JF-021 and Sutalo that Serb detainees and detainees who had Serbs intervene on their behalf were released. I also refer Your Honours to the confidential evidence table at D10 for evidence that lists were generated for the purpose of ejecting non-Serbs. The record further demonstrates that these crimes were part of a widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population which had a nexus to the armed conflict. I refer Your Honours to the confidential evidence table at D11 for a statement about the scale of the crimes. All of the crimes were perpetrated by a JCE member directly or through physical perpetrators who were used as tools of a JCE member. In addition to Arkan's Men and the SBWS TO, another armed unit which would participate in crimes together with Arkan's Men was known as the Serb National Security or SNB, the SNB is among the Serb forces listed in paragraph 6 of the indictment, it was a Special Police Unit formed by Hadzic to provide security for the government but which had broad authority to engage in other tasks. Both C-15 and JF-035 have testified about this unit. The evidence indicates that Hadzic met with the unit's commander, Stevo Bogic on a daily basis. He received reports and provided instructions. Bogic was also Hadzic's kum and a member in his government, as you saw in P16. The SNB closely collaborated with Arkan's Men in the arrest, killing and looting of non-Serb civilians in and around Erdut. The liability for three murders charged in paragraph 38, which were physically perpetrated solely by the SNB, is linked to the accused both through Arkan whose men co-operated with the SNB and requested that they kill the family, and through Hadzic who instructed his men to co-operate with Arkan's Men in committing crimes. Arkan's crimes are crimes that were intended by the JCE. The sources of information were so plentiful that the only reasonable conclusion is that the accused knew exactly what Arkan was doing it as he was doing it. In fact, the evidence leads to the conclusion that the JCE plan involved sending Arkan to commit these crimes, precisely because he advanced the JCE's purpose so effectively. Arkan's criminal background was known to Jovica Stanisic, even before he was sent to the SBWS. The state security of Serbia essentially did a background check on him, they received a full and detailed report about his criminal charges already in January 1991, admitted as P1646. Once Arkan was in the region, they knew that he was murdering prisoners and civilians. It was no secret. Arkan even gave a television interview in the autumn of 1991 stating that he does not take prisoners, which Your Honours have admitted as P326. In addition, the JNA security organ wrote numerous reports about Arkan's crimes. P1188 states that: "Arkan is engaged in the slaughter of the prisoners sent by the local territorial units." P1076 recommends that the problems should be raised at the level of the federal organs and official organs of the Republic of Serbia. Other such reports about Arkan's crimes are found in P327, P1647, and P1078. P1078 also states that: "It is known that Raznjatovic is openly supported by the MUP, TO and MNO, Ministry of Defence, of the Republic of Serbia." Additional reports --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Additional reports about the support and co-operation between Arkan and the MUP and DB are contained in P327, P1061, P1075, P1077, P1651, and D31. Your Honours, I also refer you to T-1999 to 2000 and P25, paragraph 9, for evidence from a witness who was held in Arkan's training centre and heard Arkan say that he was awaiting an order from Belgrade about what to do next. The local police could not put a stop to Arkan's crimes because the people with the most power in the SBWS were those who sent -- were those who were sent by Serbia or under their control, namely Hadzic, Badza, Kojic, Kostic, and Arkan himself. Simply put, all roads led back to the accused and the Serbian leadership. The relationship and constant co-ordination between the JCE members, Hadzic, Badza, and Arkan, as described by many witnesses is further evidence of the implementation of the JCE. In addition, the Prosecution directs the Chamber's attention to the confidential evidence table at D12 and D13. Rather than putting a stop to the crimes, quite the opposite, the accused took action to ensure that Arkan and the others could and would continue to commit them. Stanisic had the ability to influence Hadzic in his actions, as clearly demonstrated by the abundance of evidence about Hadzic's meetings with Stanisic and Milosevic, and the material support he relied on. Stanisic also had the ability to order Badza, who was in the command of the entire TO and police forces, to put a stop to Arkan's crimes. To the contrary, Badza and Hadzic provided forces to collaborate with these men and as you've heard from Mr. Bakrac, Arkan was in fact carrying out Badza's orders. Throughout the years that followed, as these armed men crossed in and out of Serbia, Stanisic and Simatovic, who were in charge of the borders, did nothing to stop them and continued to fund and arm them. Slide 47 identifies some of the key evidence about the contributions which the accused made to the JCE as implemented in the SBWS in 1991 and 1992. Much of the same evidence also supported findings that the accused planned and ordered the crimes. In addition to this evidence already discussed, there is yet another component that demonstrates Stanisic and Simatovic's contribution and their responsibility for planning subsequent crimes. Stanisic and Simatovic established two DB training camps in the region during that period. The first discussed by both JF-036 and C-15 was initially set up by Captain Dragan in Tito's castle in Tikves in July or August 1991. Your Honours have heard from Mr. Weber about Captain Dragan's relationship with the Serbian DB. There is evidence that members of this unit killed five civilians from Grabovac, a nearby location also in SBWS in May 1992, causing their family members to flee. The second camp discussed by Bogunovic was located in Ilok, also known as Pajzos. Mr. Simatovic set up the camp in Ilok in December 1991 and D33 corroborates the existence of both camps. The JCE's intent was to forcibly remove the non-Serb population from both Croatia and Bosnia. Subsequent developments in the region bear this out. The SAO SBWS and SAO Krajina were successfully merged into the Republika Srpska Krajina or RSK in February 1992. Hadzic served as the first president, followed by Milan Martic, who you've heard about from Mr. Weber. This next step was again implemented, in part by continued consultation between Milosevic, Stanisic, Hadzic, and Martic. According to JF-032, Kostic and Kojic, the DB operatives who were so key in SAO SBWS were appointed as assistants to Martic in 1992 when he became minister of interior of the RSK. Further, as cited in the confidential evidence table at D14, local RSK police initially received payment from the Serbian MUP until the Krajina dinars came into effect and they received letters stating that they were Serbian MUP employees. In addition, you will hear from my colleagues that DB trained units and instructors continued to engage in campaigns of ethnic cleansing in Bosnia. And Arkan's unit's relationship with the DB, clearly at play already in SBWS, became formalised. Your Honours, I will now hand over to Ms. Harbour who will discuss the crimes perpetrated in Bosnia in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I will address the accused's liability for crimes in Bosnia in 1992. Forcible transfer, deportation and persecution in Bijeljina, and these counts in addition to murder in Zvornik, Bosanski Samac and Doboj, all as part of a widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population during an armed conflict. For any single one of these three operations, whether the operation in Zvornik and Bijeljina or in Bosanski Samac or in Doboj, the evidence is sufficient that Stanisic and Simatovic could be convicted on all five counts of the indictment. Before discussing their liability for these crimes through their role in the JCE and by planning and ordering, I will discuss the context in which these crimes were committed revealing why they were integral to the JCE's common criminal plan. In order to effectuate the common criminal plan in Bosnia, the Bosnian Serb leadership made several policy decisions that would dictate the focus of the JCE members' efforts. On 19 December 1991, the SDS leadership issued the Variant A and B instructions. The objective was to separate the ethnic Serbs from non-Serbs by organising Serb local governments, police forces, and Territorial Defences. This fed into the Bosnian Serb leadership's six strategic goals. Mr. Farr mentioned the first goal, which in essence articulates the common plan: The separation of the Serb people from the other two ethnic communities entailing the permanent removal of a significant part of the non-Serb population. The crimes committed in Bosnia in the first half of 1992 targeted areas that would also further the second and third strategic goals, which together aimed to connect Serbia and the Serbian territories in Bosnia to the Serbian territories in Croatia by establishing control over the so-called Posavina corridor. The Serbs targeted Bijeljina, Zvornik, Bosanski Samac, and Doboj because of their location along the Posavina corridor. By the time Karadzic officially articulated these goals on 12 May 1992, the accused and other members of the JCE had already significantly contributed to achieving them. The Prosecution's case is that Stanisic and Simatovic, through their leadership roles in the Serbian DB, planned the take-over of Bijeljina and Zvornik intending to drive the non-Serb population out through the crimes of forcible transfer, deportation, murder, and persecution. On the orders of Stanisic and Simatovic, Arkan co-ordinated with other forces including Seselj's men, the JNA, local TOs, and Serb paramilitaries to implement the common criminal plan. And following the take-over, Stanisic and Simatovic ordered their tool, Marko Pavlovic, as Zvornik TO commander, to finish the job, co-ordinating mass deportations through the Serbian MUP. Before the attack on Bijeljina and Zvornik, the Serb leadership was preparing for ethnic division, creating and implementing policies that discriminated against the non-Serb population, listed at slide 49 and at E1 through E3 of the confidential evidence table. From 1991, sources in Serbia armed Zvornik's Serbs. Zvornik received arms from the police and JNA legally and illegally. Radmilo Bogdanovic, a member of the JCE and Rade Kostic, who, as Ms. Friedman discussed, was responsible for arms distribution in SBWS, also armed the Serbs in Zvornik by organising weapons transfers from Croatia. I refer Your Honours to the confidential evidence table at E4. At the end of March 1992, the Serbian DB under Stanisic's authority gave orders to take control over Bijeljina and Zvornik in rapid succession. On 31 March, Arkan's Tigers entered Bijeljina and in co-ordination with the Bijeljina TO and paramilitaries took control of the town. The Serb forces began a persecutory campaign of violence targeting Bosnian Muslim civilians. In this context, Muslim civilians evacuated Bijeljina. As one witness stated, whoever could leave, left. And this is E5 on the confidential evidence table. By the time JCE member Biljana Plavsic came to Bijeljina on 4 April, Serb flags waved from two mosques. Plavsic greeted Arkan with a kiss. For the evidence on Bijeljina, I refer the Chamber to slide 50 and the confidential evidence table at E6. Soon after, during a meeting of the Zvornik Crisis Staff, Plavsic asked that Arkan be called to assist Zvornik as well. Through Radmilo Bogdanovic and Kostic, the Zvornik police arranged to meet with Arkan who immediately sent his deputy and around 20 of his Tigers to Zvornik. Around 7 April Arkan met with the head of the Muslim police in Zvornik. In his own words: "I gave them an ultimatum to surrender the town by 0800 hours; otherwise I would destroy it. That's how it was." This is P1601, page 3. Asked who masterminded the Zvornik attack, JCE member Seselj said: "It was key people of the State Security Service who thought it up, among them Franko Simatovic, Frenki. He was also one of the key executors." This is from P18, page 29. Arkan's Men attacked Zvornik as the Serbian DB planned and ordered on 8 April. Consistent with the JCE, Arkan's Tigers co-ordinated this effort with JNA units and Serb paramilitaries. The JNA provided tanks, artillery, mortars to Arkan's Men. Before attacking, JNA General Jankovic received a letter from a private citizen describing Arkan's ultimatum and foretelling "unprecedented massacre of the unprotected and innocent population." The letter pleaded with the JNA not to align with the forces threatening the population, but instead to defend the population. This is P1380. The JNA disregarded this plea, instead combining with Arkan's Men and the paramilitaries to crush Zvornik's Muslim population. As one witness described, during and following the take-over, Arkan's unit, the Serb Crisis Staff, and the JNA became aggressive and ethnically cleansed the area in order to create territories inhabited by a majority of Serbs. This is E7 on the confidential evidence table. For evidence regarding the Zvornik attack, I refer Your Honours to the evidence of JF-026, Theunens' expert report P1575 beginning at e-court page 336, and E6 on the confidential evidence table.
